opus-5.5.text:
I think the core problem Taichi tries to solve is a kind of mismatch between how people *think* about simulation and how they have to *write* it to make it fast.

When you're doing physical simulation — say fluids, elastic bodies, snow, smoke — the math is often quite elegant. You have particles, you have grids, you transfer quantities between them, you solve some equations. But if you want that to run at scale, on a GPU, with millions or hundreds of millions of degrees of freedom, suddenly you're dealing with memory layouts, sparse data structures, thread scheduling, cache behavior, CUDA kernels, all of that. And in practice, a researcher might spend most of their time on the engineering rather than the physics.

During my PhD at MIT, I felt this pain very personally. I'd have an idea for a new simulation method, and implementing a high-performance version could take weeks or months. And a lot of that code was not reusable — you hand-optimize one sparse grid structure, and then if you want to change the data layout, you almost rewrite everything.

So the idea behind Taichi was to decouple these concerns. You write the computation in a fairly high-level way — it's embedded in Python, so it feels approachable — and then the compiler takes care of mapping it to efficient code on different backends: CPUs, CUDA, Vulkan, Metal, and so on. A key piece is that data structures, especially spatially sparse ones, are treated as first-class. You can describe the hierarchy of your sparse grid separately from the algorithm, and the compiler generates the access code and optimizations for you. That's something that's really important for large-scale simulation, because the interesting regions of space are usually sparse — a fluid only occupies part of the domain, for example.

Later we also added things like differentiable programming, so you can get gradients through a simulation, which opens doors for learning and optimization and control.

So if I summarize it in one sentence: Taichi is trying to let people write simulation code close to how they think, while still getting performance close to what an expert would hand-tune. It's lowering the barrier so that more people — researchers, artists, students — can actually build these large-scale physical worlds without becoming GPU performance engineers first.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that the infrastructure problem in simulation was never really about math. The equations for fluids, soft bodies, granular materials, all of that has been understood for decades. The problem was that turning those equations into something that runs fast on real hardware required a completely different skill set than the one the people writing the equations had.

When I was doing my PhD at MIT, I'd watch this pattern over and over. A graphics or physics researcher would have a beautiful idea, something like a new material point method variant, and they'd prototype it in Python or MATLAB. It would take hours to simulate a few seconds of footage. So then they'd rewrite it in C++, hand-vectorize it, maybe port it to CUDA, and suddenly they're spending three months on memory layouts and thread synchronization instead of on the actual physics. And the moment they wanted to change the data structure, say from a dense grid to a sparse one to handle large empty regions, everything had to be rewritten. The algorithm and the implementation were completely tangled together.

So the core idea behind Taichi was to decouple those two things. You write the computation at a high level, as if you were just describing the physics, loops over particles, loops over grid cells. And separately, you describe how data is laid out in memory, whether it's dense, sparse, hierarchical, what the block sizes are. The compiler then takes both and generates efficient code for whatever backend you're targeting, CPU, GPU, whatever. That means the same simulation code can run on a laptop for prototyping and then scale to a big GPU without you touching the algorithm.

The other piece people underestimate is sparsity. Most large-scale simulations are mostly empty space. A fluid splash occupies a tiny fraction of the bounding box. If your data structure can't skip empty regions efficiently, you're wasting the vast majority of your compute and memory. But writing sparse data structures by hand is painful and error-prone, which is why most people just didn't. Making that a first-class language feature was probably the thing that let Taichi handle scales that were previously out of reach for a single researcher.

And then there's differentiability. Once you have a compiler sitting between the user's code and the hardware, you can do source-to-source automatic differentiation through the whole simulator. That opened up a lot of things in learning and control that would have been impractical otherwise, because nobody wants to hand-derive gradients through a thousand timesteps of a physics solver.

So in short, the problem I was trying to solve was productivity. Let the person who understands the physics write the physics, and let the system worry about making it fast.

astra-6.text:
I think the infrastructure problem is that expressing a simulation and making it run efficiently are two very different tasks. You may have a clear mathematical model, but once you want to run it at a large scale, you have to think about parallel execution, memory layout, and how to use the hardware effectively. That can become a much bigger engineering effort than implementing the model itself.

The idea behind Taichi is to separate those concerns. You describe the computation in a way that is close to the simulation you want to build, and the compiler handles much of the work of translating that into efficient execution. It doesn’t eliminate the need to understand performance, but it gives you a common foundation so you don’t have to rebuild that infrastructure for every new simulation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the infrastructure problem is really the gap between describing a simulation and making it run efficiently at scale. You might have a physical model that is quite simple mathematically, but implementing it on modern hardware requires a lot of work: parallelization, memory management, data structures, and hardware-specific optimization.

With Taichi, the idea is to separate those concerns. You describe the computation in a relatively intuitive way, and the compiler handles much of the work of turning that into efficient parallel code. That lets researchers and engineers spend more time on the simulation itself, while still getting the performance they need to tackle larger problems.
